## Analysis at each round
### Round 1
There are no trials yet. The starting architecture scored 0.000 on both seeds, so we can't yet tell whether the bottleneck is the recipe or the network's representation. At the default recipe, each update is 4096 steps and the budget allows only about 32 updates. That is very few PPO updates for a placement policy with about 257 actions, so smaller rollouts and more updates are an obvious first lever. On the structure side, a good placement needs three things. First, the landing layer, which is the maximum build height under the footprint. Second, all footprint cells at that layer must be missing from the build. Third, no missing cells may be left trapped below. The starting net uses 2D features only, so it has to compress the layer index into channels. A per-layer branch that pools over each footprint and then takes a max over layers should learn this check more easily. Round 1 tests the recipe on the baseline, then the layer-aware net with that recipe, then the same net with fewer epochs and more samples.

### Round 2
All three trials scored 0 on both seeds, and training success over the last 10% of training was also 0. Changing the recipe (83 updates) did not help, and neither did the layer-aware footprint head, so the runs give no ranking yet. The agent seems never to learn accurate enough single placements to finish a full design. Under a fixed compute budget, the number of gradient steps grows as the minibatch shrinks, and fewer epochs buy fresher samples. The default makes about 4k gradient steps of 128 samples each; r1c1 made only about 2k. The next round therefore tests a much more aggressive recipe: 64 envs × 16 steps, 2 epochs and minibatches of 64. That gives about 7k gradient steps and over 150 updates. I apply it to the baseline and to the layer-aware net, so the two results are directly comparable. A third, new architecture shares learned 3x3 convs across layers and uses learned footprint-shaped convs instead of fixed pooling. It hedges against the world differing from its description.

### Round 3
All six trials scored 0 on dev and 0 on train (last 10%). This covers the baseline and two layer-aware heads, across recipes with 32 to 225 updates and 1.6k to 7k gradient steps. Because train success is also 0, the problem is learning, not generalisation. Neither update count nor the r1c2 per-layer pooling has helped. A key rule seems to be missing from the inputs: a brick is correct only if it lands at layer L, every footprint cell is missing at L, and nothing is still missing below L in those columns. Earlier per-layer branches saw only neighbouring layers, so 'no missing cell below' was hard to compute. Plan: give each layer its whole column in layer-relative order, where that rule is a simple linear threshold. Use 1 PPO epoch to get about 2 to 3 times more fresh samples. Two controls go with it: a symmetric 3x3 head, in case the anchor or footprint convention differs from the description, and a 2-epoch recipe.

### Round 4
All 9 trials scored 0 on dev and 0 on train success. That includes the baseline under three recipes and three layer-aware designs. Noise cannot explain this. The layer-aware designs depended on the documented channel layout, anchor convention and footprints, and they did no better than the generic baseline. So either the budget is far too small, or the world differs from its description in a way that hand-built structure misreads, such as the action layout or the anchor and footprint convention. Ending at the right moment with DONE is another likely barrier. Only global mean and max features currently see whether nothing is missing, and the critic is weak. With one round left, I am spreading the bets. Candidate 1 runs the baseline with 1 epoch for the most samples (about 400k). Candidate 2 is a generic deeper CNN that assumes no anchor convention, with learned 3x3 type heads and a detector feeding DONE. Candidate 3 adds a fully connected head that assumes no action layout and gives the critic a view of the whole board.
